# Agent instructions

## Working preferences

Always apply these, in any project:

- **No meta-commentary inside artifacts.** Deliverables (documents, code, files) must read as standalone, finished work - never narrating how they were made or what changed. Avoid phrases like "as requested", "for consistency", "this section now covers...", "I added...". Notes about what was done belong in the chat reply, and only when asked at the time. Genuine reader aids (e.g. "See the Glossary for definitions") are fine; commentary about the artifact's own editing is not.

- **Plain ASCII characters.** Do not use characters people rarely type by hand. Use a hyphen (or a double hyphen where grammatically apt) instead of an em-dash or en-dash; a comma or "/" instead of a middot; "..." instead of an ellipsis glyph; "->" and "<->" instead of arrow glyphs. Straight quotes, not curly.

- **Parallelize what parallelizes cleanly.** When subtasks are independent, run them concurrently - parallel tool calls, fan-out workers, background jobs - rather than serially. Keep genuinely dependent steps in order; default to parallel, and fall back to serial only for a real dependency or a shared resource that would conflict.

- **Investigate and design up front, then push the build down.** Do the exploration, the architecture, and the decisions in the main context, where the whole problem is in view. Then cut the work into units that do not overlap and give each one to its own subagent, with a brief that carries the decisions already made (4.6), so no one re-derives them or re-opens a settled question. Keep the design, the integration, and the final review at the top; push the mechanical build-out down. Delegate only what is specified well enough for a fresh context to finish without guessing - when you cannot write that brief, the investigation is not finished.

- **Right-size the model and the effort.** Use the smallest model and the lowest reasoning effort that still does the job well. Give small and simple work - a rename, a lookup, a single-file edit, a mechanical sweep - to Haiku, and check what comes back every time. Raise the tier for work that needs judgment: design, review, debugging, and anything whose shape is not yet clear. When you are not sure which tier fits, default to Sonnet at extra-high effort. Verification is part of the choice, not an optional extra: a wrong answer from a cheap model costs more than the tokens it saved.

- **Simplified Technical English for prose.** Write all non-code prose - tickets, documentation, comments, commit messages, and the like - to ASD-STE100 (Simplified Technical English): short sentences, one main clause, active voice, approved-dictionary vocabulary (one word per meaning, one meaning per word, used the same way every time), and no unnecessary jargon or idiom. Code itself (identifiers, syntax) is unaffected.

## Engineering standards

Project-level delivery gates for any codebase. These are not style; they are the bar for calling work done. Hold to all of them.

### 1. Tests

- **1.1 Test-driven.** Write the failing test first and confirm it fails for the real reason (red), make it pass (green), then refactor. Do not write the implementation first and backfill tests to match it. Commit the failing tests before the implementation - that commit is the spec.
- **1.2 Spec-based and realistic.** Tests express the behavior and contract, not the implementation. Cover realistic technical and business edge cases - boundaries, empty/null, concurrency, failure and rollback paths, malformed input - not just the happy path.
- **1.3 Coverage is a floor, not a target.** Enforce a coverage minimum in CI, but never write hollow tests to hit a number. Unit tests are deterministic: no real network, clock, filesystem, or randomness - inject them.
- **1.4 Acceptance criteria as named tests.** Turn each acceptance criterion into its own named test whose name is legible from the test output, so a failing run names the unmet requirement rather than just a line number.
- **1.5 Mock external APIs from captured fixtures.** Tests never call a live external API. Mock the API at the client boundary and drive the mock from fixture files. Capture each fixture from the real API where at all possible, then anonymize it per 5.3: replace names, identifiers, tokens, and PII, but keep the true response shape, the full field set, and realistic value formats. Prefer a captured-and-scrubbed fixture over a hand-written one, because hand-written payloads drift from what the service actually returns. Capture the error, empty, and rate-limit responses too, not only the success case. Record the API version and the capture date next to the fixture, and re-capture when the API changes. When capture is impossible - no access, no sandbox account - build the fixture from the published schema or the documented example and note which fixtures are unverified.

### 2. Types and data modeling

- **2.1 Warnings are errors.** Configure warnings-as-errors at the compiler/interpreter level for every language in the project (e.g. `-Werror`, `-D warnings`, strict/error lint levels). Enforce it mechanically in the build config, not by reviewer vigilance. Never bypass the gate with `--no-verify` or by disabling a hook; if a hook is genuinely broken, fix it in its own change. Pre-existing warnings in a file you touch are yours to clear, not to build on.
- **2.2 Static type checking in strict mode** where the language supports it (mypy/pyright strict, `tsc --noEmit`, and the like), run as part of the gate. It catches a different class of defect than the linter.
- **2.3 Model data with types.** Represent modeled data as declared types (classes, dataclasses, structs, records, Pydantic models), not loose maps. In dynamic languages such as Python, use classes rather than dictionaries when modeling data with a known shape; reserve dictionaries for genuinely dynamic key/value collections.
- **2.4 Enums and schemas for data shapes.** Model a fixed set of valid values as an enum (or the language equivalent), not bare strings or ints, so invalid states are hard to represent. For data that crosses the network, define it with a schema or IDL - protocol buffers or similar - and generate the types rather than hand-rolling ad hoc transfer shapes. Document every field and type in the schema (proto comments and the like) so the contract is self-explaining.

### 3. Definition of Done

Work is not done until all of the following hold; the mechanical checks in 3.1 run the same way locally and in CI:

- **3.1 Format, lint, type-check, and test - all green.** No skipped or disabled checks. When a check fails, fix the code to meet accurate tests, or adjust tests to match new realities the user has confirmed - never weaken the gate to pass. Do not disable or ignore a test you broke; fix it, or open a tracked follow-up and reference it from the skip.
- **3.2 Docs updated** to reflect the new reality (READMEs, API docs, comments, changelogs) in the same change.
- **3.3 Adversarial review from fresh eyes, two passes.** Review the work adversarially for correctness, security, structure, and maintainability (modularity, file size, naming, control flow, comments). Run the review from a fresh context - a separate agent, session, or person that did not produce the work - because the author carries the same blind spots into the review. Give the reviewer the requirement and the diff, not the author's reasoning. Where you run more than one reviewer, give each a distinct lens - correctness, security, performance, operability, does-the-failure-actually-reproduce - rather than repeating one pass, because separate lenses catch what a repeated pass cannot. Triage findings by severity and fix them, then review the fixes in a second pass. Anything deliberately left unfixed gets a one-line recorded reason. This applies to every deliverable, not only code: designs, documents, schemas, and infrastructure definitions get the same two passes against their own bar - for a design, that is whether it meets the stated requirements and survives the failure cases.
- **3.4 A finding must survive refutation.** The burden of proof sits on the finding, not on the code. Before you act on one, try to kill it: name the concrete failure - the inputs, the state, and the wrong result - and check it against the code. Drop it when you cannot show that failure. Findings that are expensive to fix, or that would change the design, get an independent check from someone who did not raise them. Plausible-but-wrong findings are the main failure mode of adversarial review, and they cost more than the defects they claim to find.
- **3.5 No silent caps.** Report the limits of the work you did. When you sample, stop at the first N, skip a directory, disable a flaky check, or abandon a path, say so plainly in the summary, the PR description, or the tracker entry. Silent truncation reads as full coverage to whoever receives the result, and they cannot see the gap that you saw. "I checked the three largest callers, not all forty" is a useful result; "I checked the callers" is not.

### 4. Workflow and change hygiene

- **4.1 Scope.** Change only what the task requires. Unrelated issues you notice become tracker entries, not inline edits.
- **4.2 Commits.** Small and atomic, with conventional-commit messages. Never commit with a failing gate or bundle unrelated changes. Commit lockfiles.
- **4.3 Branch and PR.** Do new work on a branch, not directly on `main`; commit and push there freely. When it is ready, open a pull request and ask the user whether they want to review it - do not merge to `main` unprompted. This strict default holds unless a repo overrides it in its own `AGENTS.md` (for example authorizing merge-when-green via PR, or direct merges of green, independently-shippable changes). (Uses the `gh` CLI; where it is unavailable, push the branch and hand off the merge.)
- **4.4 Isolated worktrees.** Do code work in a dedicated git worktree on its own branch off the base (usually `origin/main`), never in the repo's primary checkout - so concurrent sessions never collide on the working tree, branch checkout, or build artifacts. Run edits, builds, tests, and commits from that worktree; place it at `<repo>/.worktrees/<branch>/` (or the repo group's own convention) and remove it after merge. Leave another session's in-flight worktree alone - inspect it read-only, but do not edit, commit, or switch its branch. Where the tooling supports subagents, give each unit of work its own fresh agent in its own worktree: a fresh agent carries no stale assumptions from earlier work, and the separate worktree lets the agents run at the same time without collision. Exceptions, stated then handled: the target is not a git repo, the task is read-only or non-code, or a path dependency makes a worktree impractical.
- **4.5 Keep `main` releasable.** `main` must build, test, and run at every commit. Favor small, green, independently-shippable changes - additive, behavior-preserving, or behind a default that preserves the old path - over batching work into a large release, and do not hold ready work back needlessly (how a change actually reaches `main`, direct or via PR with review, follows 4.3 and any repo override). Land co-dependent changes together and name the interlock ("blocked-by #X", "must merge with #Y") so it is visible without reading the diff. When in doubt, hold: a half-coupled change that breaks `main` costs everyone.
- **4.6 Brief the worker; do not make it re-derive.** When you hand work to a fresh agent or person, give them what they need to start: the problem and why it matters, the files and interfaces in play, the constraints, and the acceptance criteria that say when the work is done. Rediscovery is the main cost of a fresh context, so pay it once in the brief instead of once per worker. Point at the tracker entry (9.3) rather than repeating it. One thing stays out of the brief when you want independent judgment: your own conclusion about the answer, which a reviewer (3.3) must never receive.
- **4.7 Search until dry, and search several ways.** For work of unknown size - finding every call site, hunting bugs, enumerating edge cases, auditing - do not stop at a count you chose in advance. Keep going until two rounds in a row find nothing new. Search along independent axes, because each axis is blind to what the others find: symbol name, string literal, import and dependency graph, configuration and templates, and git history. One grep is not coverage. State which axes you ran (3.5).

### 5. Security and data safety

- **5.1 Secrets and input safety.** Never commit secrets - keep them in a secret manager (or env vars) and reference them appropriately, and run a secret scan in the gate. Validate and parameterize all external input (no string-built SQL, shell, or paths).
- **5.2 No local-environment or personal data in the repo.** Never write machine- or person-specific details into anything that lands in git - code, configs, manifests, docs, comments, commit messages, or PR descriptions. This covers internal hostnames and domains, IP addresses, usernames, absolute home paths, personal ports, emails, account/cluster IDs, and registry or service URLs. Use workspace-relative paths and pull anything machine-specific from configuration or the environment, and substitute obvious placeholders in examples (`registry.example.com`, `example.com`, `user@example.com`, `/home/<user>` or `$HOME`, `192.0.2.0/24`). Values common to the shared cloud or CI environment are fine; a specific dev box is not. Scan the diff for real hostnames, IPs, paths, and emails before committing.
- **5.3 No real client data.** Never commit real client or production data to the repo. Test fixtures are fine, but they must use synthetic, anonymized, or clearly fake data - never real records, PII, or customer content. Generate or scrub fixtures; do not copy from production.

### 6. Dependencies and reproducibility

- **6.1 Dependencies.** Justify each new dependency, prefer the standard library, and pin versions. When adding one, check the current release with tooling (e.g. `npm view`, `pip index versions`, `cargo search`, your package manager's latest-version query) and use an up-to-date, maintained version rather than one cached or remembered. Scan for known vulnerabilities before the first build, because install and build scripts (`npm` postinstall, cargo `build.rs`, and the like) execute code at build time. A high or critical advisory is a hard blocker, not a note for later: patch it in the same change, or prove the path unreachable and record why, or file a tracked entry and reference it from the change. Never ship past one silently, and never pin around one without a comment or a tracked entry. A new dependency is a review item.
- **6.2 Reproducibility and local parity.** Pin the toolchain; a fresh clone plus one documented command builds and tests, with no reliance on machine-local state. Maintain local development tooling that runs and tests the system end to end as far as is practical - containers (Docker/Podman), a local Kubernetes (k3s/kind), LocalStack, and the like - created early and kept current as the system grows. A working local run-and-test loop is part of the Definition of Done, not a later add-on.
- **6.3 Command runner.** Use `just` as the task runner; expose the common targets in a `justfile` (for example `check`, `test`, `dev`) that both people and CI call. Keep it simple - recipes stay short. When a recipe's logic grows long, put it in a script under `scripts/` and call that script from the recipe rather than inlining it.

### 7. Architecture and code structure

- **7.1 Clean separation of concerns.** Separate transport and requests from services and domain logic (ports and adapters / hexagonal, adapted to the situation). Business logic depends only on its own domain types and abstractions - never on transport, framework, ORM, or other systems' types; push those to adapters at the edges and map to domain types. Keep the domain cleanly unit-testable in isolation, without standing up infrastructure.
- **7.2 File size and modularity.** Keep code files under about 1000 lines where practical; when one grows past that, split it into submodules along clear responsibility lines. Test files are exempt where the language idiom keeps tests in-file.
- **7.3 Earn abstractions.** Do not introduce a new abstraction until about three call sites prove the pattern; premature indirection is harder to remove than to add. When a single new type unifies several existing needs, justify the unification explicitly rather than assuming generality is free. Reuse existing abstractions and the established layering before inventing parallel ones.
- **7.4 Compare candidate designs before you commit.** For a design decision with a wide solution space, produce two or three independent candidates from different angles - the simplest thing that works, the lowest-risk option, the best fit for the change you expect next - before you choose one. Score them against the stated requirements and the failure cases, then build the winner and graft in the good ideas from the others. Record the choice and the reason where the design lives. One attempt then iterated converges on the first idea you had, not the best one available. Skip this where the shape is already fixed by the existing system.

### 8. Errors, status, and reliability

- **8.1 Errors.** No swallowed exceptions or ignored error returns. Fail loud with actionable messages; log at boundaries with structure.
- **8.2 Operational declines are not failures.** Distinguish a normal business outcome (e.g. a REST API returning a rules-based refusal, or a 4xx for a known condition) from a genuine failure (misconfiguration, timeout, dependency outage, unexpected 5xx). Reserve error-level logs and thrown errors for issues that actually need attention; record expected declines as normal-path outcomes (info/debug, or a domain result), not errors. When it is unclear which a case is, ask rather than guessing.
- **8.3 Business status in the payload, not the protocol.** When designing APIs, do not signal business-rule outcomes through protocol-level failure codes (e.g. HTTP 4xx in REST). Return a success transport status (HTTP 200) unless there was a technical failure, in which case use the appropriate 4xx/5xx. Carry the business outcome in the response body: a top-level `status` of `OK` or `FAILED`, plus a structured result with a business status code, a description, a user-facing message, and a `retryable` flag - so a caller can tell a business failure from a technical one unambiguously.
- **8.4 Idempotent operations.** All operations must be idempotent: repeating the same request with the same inputs yields the same result and no additional side effects. Use idempotency keys, natural keys, or upserts for writes so retries and redeliveries are safe by design.

### 9. Issue tracker

- **9.1 Establish the tracker once.** The first time you do project work and the tracker is unknown, ask which issue tracker the project uses (Jira, GitHub Issues, Linear, etc.) and how to access it. Record the answer in the repo's own `AGENTS.md` - the tracker name, its location or URL, and how to create and update entries. Never record it in a generated file such as `AGENTS.base.md`, because the next sync overwrites that file and the answer is lost. From then on treat it as fixed and stop asking.
- **9.2 Outstanding work lives in the tracker,** not in code comments or memory. Anything deferred, discovered, or out of scope becomes an entry.
- **9.3 Entries assume fresh eyes.** Each entry gives someone who knows nothing about it - a fresh agent or human - enough to pick it up: what the work is, why it is needed, and acceptance criteria. Well-structured and complete on the critical details, but not verbose.
- **9.4 Keep entries current.** Claim or self-assign an entry when you start it so parallel work does not collide, and as work progresses update the tracker: status/state, the current owner, and a short comment capturing decisions, blockers, and what changed. The tracker should reflect reality at any moment, not just at creation and close.
- **9.5 Epics for large efforts.** A large, multi-part effort gets an epic ticket, with the individual work items as linked tickets. The epic describes what is being built at a higher level and what each linked ticket is for (a short, high-level summary per ticket); it is closed only when its sub-tickets are complete.
- **9.6 Link work to the tracker.** Reference the tracker item from the branch or PR - `Closes #N` to auto-close on merge, `Refs #N` for a partial fix - so code and tracker stay connected without manual cross-checking.
- **9.7 Status before stopping.** On multi-session or long-running work, leave a short status note before you stop - what landed, what is in progress, what is blocked, and what is next - so another agent or human can reconstruct state without replaying git log.
